title: The Bee in the Garland
story:
The Danava lords of Vajra had watched many performers, but never a troupe whose heroes looked so exactly like the heroes they were pretending to be.

Word of the actors had gone ahead of them. When the troupe reached Supura, a dependent city of the Asura king, Vajranabha's orders had already arrived: give them the finest rooms, treat them as guests, press jewels and fine raiment upon them. The actor who had won the sages' boon danced for the citizens of Supura, and they were delighted. Then the company staged the Ramayana — the birth of Vishnu for the destruction of Ravana, and how the kings Lomapada and Dasharatha brought the young sage Rishyashringa to the court of Shanta. The players personated Rama, Lakshmana, Shatrughna, and Bharata so perfectly that even the oldest Danavas were startled and spoke again and again of the resemblance. They rose from their seats to applaud and threw down necklaces of gold and vaidurya, bracelets, and cloths; and the actors, in verse, praised each Asura house in the order of its family and birth.

The news reached the city of Vajra, and Vajranabha, who had heard of the famous actor long before, sent a messenger. The Daityas of the branch cities conducted the disguised Yadavas into the great city itself. For their lodging they were given a beautiful house built by the celestial architect; and Vajranabha raised a great pavilion and made a festival of the players. When they had rested, he gave them profuse jewels and called for the play. The women of his family watched from behind a screen, and the Asura king sat with his kinsmen.

The young men of the Yadava house dressed themselves as actors and began. First came the music — kamsya, venu, and muraja; then the women of the troupe sang the Gandharva song Chhalikya, sweet to ear and mind; and with the seven scales, the three gramas, and the ragas of spring, they sang the song of the sacred descent of the Ganga, and the Asuras rose again and again in pleasure. Pradyumna, Gada, and Shamba — all in the guise of actors — conducted the nandi, the opening benediction, and Rukmini's son sang the hymn of the Ganga's descent with graceful gestures. Then came the drama Rambhabhisara: Shura played Ravana, Monovati played Rambha, Pradyumna played Nalakuvara, and Shamba played the jester. By their illusory powers the Yadavas conjured the very scene of Kailasa — how the angry Nalakuvara cursed Ravana and comforted Rambha. Scene by scene, the delighted Danavas showered the stage with costly garments, jewelled necklaces, sky-cars, celestial elephants, cool sandal and aloe scents — and at last the Chintamani, the gem that grants every wish. So freely did they give that they drained their own treasuries, the women of the Asura chiefs among them.

But the true purpose of the festival lay elsewhere. Prabhavati's friend Suchimukhi, the goose, came to the princess and said: "I went to Dwaraka, the city of the Yadavas. I saw Pradyumna there in secret and told him of your love. He was pleased, and he has appointed this evening for meeting you. The Yadavas never speak an untruth. Truly, today you will meet your love."

Prabhavati's heart leapt. "Stay in my room tonight," she told the goose. "If you are with me, I fear nobody. With you beside me, I wish to see Krishna's son."

That evening a fragrant garland, thick with bees, was carried to the princess's chamber. Hidden among the bees was Pradyumna, who had taken the form of one of them. The maids set the garland down near Prabhavati. As dusk turned to evening, the other bees flew away one by one — and the one that remained, the hero of the Yadava house, slowly settled on Prabhavati's ear.

The full moon rose, and Prabhavati, whose limbs burned and whose mouth had gone dry, confessed to the goose the strange fever she had caught from loving a man she had only heard of. "I have not seen him," she said, "and still my limbs burn." Then the bee at her ear was no bee at all — the guest promised for the evening had come. In the lamplit room above the city, the long-pining lovers met at last: the bride who had given her heart to a name, and the hero who had crossed the most guarded walls in the world in the shape of a bee in a flower-garland.
reflection: The city that no army could breach is entered by a bee in a garland. Pradyumna, who could fight any host, comes to his bride as the smallest of creatures — the episode's power lies in how much is carried by stillness and trust: a goose's promise, a princess's faith, an evening kept.
next_story_tease: The marriage was secret, but the sons it would bring into the world would not stay hidden for long.
hero_scene: By moonlight in Prabhavati's chamber, a single bee settles on the princess's ear as the rest of the garland's bees drift away into the evening; her eyes widen, half-afraid and half-knowing, as the full moon rises over the city of Vajra.
